desk-setup-back-pain.title: 5 signs your desk setup is hurting your back
desk-setup-back-pain.summary: Small ergonomic changes can end months of neck and back pain.
desk-setup-back-pain.html:
Long hours at a desk are one of the most common reasons people come to see a physiotherapist. The good news is that the body usually tells you early when your workstation is working against you. Here are five signs worth taking seriously.

1. Stiffness after sitting

If your lower back feels achy or tight when you stand up after an hour or two, your spine has probably been held in one position for too long. The body is built to move, and even a perfect chair becomes uncomfortable if you never leave it.

2. Tight neck and shoulders by mid-afternoon

A screen that sits too low or too far away pulls your head forward. Your neck and upper back muscles then work all day to hold it up, which often shows up as tension between the shoulder blades and the base of the neck.

3. Headaches that build through the day

Headaches that start at the base of the skull and creep forward as the day goes on can be linked to sustained neck posture and eye strain. They are worth mentioning to a professional, particularly if they are becoming more frequent.

4. Tingling or aching in the hands

Resting your wrists on a hard edge, typing with your elbows at an awkward angle, or gripping a mouse for hours can irritate the nerves and tendons of the forearm and hand.

5. Slumping without noticing

If you catch yourself sliding down in your chair or leaning towards the screen, your setup is probably not giving you the support you need to stay comfortable.

Simple changes to try

  • Raise your screen so the top sits around eye level, roughly an arm’s length away.
  • Keep your elbows near 90 degrees with your forearms supported.
  • Place your feet flat on the floor or on a footrest.
  • Stand, walk or stretch for a minute or two every 30 to 45 minutes.
  • Vary your position through the day rather than searching for one perfect posture.

When to see a physiotherapist

If discomfort lasts more than a couple of weeks, keeps returning, wakes you at night, or comes with numbness, tingling or weakness, it is time to have it assessed. An ergonomic assessment at Revive Wellness looks at your workstation, your movement and your habits, and gives you a plan that fits your working day.

strength-training-after-50.title: Muscle Is Medicine: Why Building Muscle Is the Secret to Ageing Well
strength-training-after-50.summary: Muscle is far more than show. It is a health marker that shapes how well you age.
strength-training-after-50.html:
In the world of modern bodybuilding, people tend to picture big muscles with limited mobility - all show and no function.

Many question the purpose and importance of building muscle, aka hypertrophy. Especially in Asia, where the social standard of beauty favors a slim, slender look.

But as mankind lives longer and modern society faces population aging, longevity is directly linked to how much muscle you have and how well you can preserve it.

Muscles are not just dumb objects clinging to bones. Muscle is a health marker. It reflects how well your body metabolizes energy, how well it responds to insulin and regulates blood sugar, and even how it supports cognitive function.

Our movements depend on muscles lengthening, shortening, and contracting isometrically. Our muscles respond to force and stress from gravity. How we use our muscles determines the outcome. For example, prolonged sitting causes muscle atrophy, while resistance training drives muscle growth. In short: use it or lose it.

When we move under specific loads, our muscles experience different types of growth. One fascinating aspect of our physiology is what happens in the lengthened position under load. During a stretch under load, our body experiences longitudinal growth - in simple terms, the muscle fibers grow longer near the tendons, close to the joint attachments.

In our next post, we'll talk about how longitudinal growth protects our tendons and why most bodybuilding research is actually based on rehab.

return-to-sport-after-injury.title: Back in the Game: How to Return to Sport After Injury Safely
return-to-sport-after-injury.summary: Sports injury rehab, return-to-play testing and reinjury prevention, explained by a Hong Kong physiotherapist.
return-to-sport-after-injury.html:
When people hear of football, rugby and other sports, a fair few will associate sports with injury, or recall the time they could have turned professional if it wasn’t for a devastating injury. When you watch football, after a collision, a team of physios and other members of the medical staff rush onto the pitch with their duffel bags filled with medical equipment.

From a physio’s perspective, we are the bridge between the medical doctors and personal training, facilitating everything from and in-between. We are required to have a medical background, such as anatomy, the healing phases of different connective tissue, therapeutic modalities and treatments, as well as knowledge about physical activity: how to apply the medical knowledge to real-world scenarios with the equipment we are given.

I’ll give you a brief example:

Picture this: you are in the middle of a match when your knee twists awkwardly beneath you. Within minutes it swells up, and your gut tells you this is bad. You cannot carry on, so you hobble off the pitch.

You go to see a doctor, who prescribes painkillers and anti-inflammatories, and refers you to physiotherapy. This is where we come in. A physiotherapist’s job is not just to assess the injury; it starts with listening to your story and what happened, and asking questions to get a clearer picture first. We may then guide you through some basic movements, assess your balance, strength and pain levels, and carry out special tests to confirm, or rule out, the cause.

We also have to communicate our findings and our thought process clearly with you, to keep the dialogue open and stop you from guessing or becoming even more worried. From there, treatment could range from controlling the swelling first, to reducing pain levels, to relaxing muscles that are guarding as a protective mechanism. It is also about calming your nerves and reassuring you that things are going to be fine.

After that, physiotherapy should mainly be about tailoring an exercise programme around your needs: neuromuscular control, balance, proprioception, agility, muscle strength and psychological readiness, pushing you to a reasonable limit each session.

But the journey doesn’t end there. Even after you get back to the sport you love, physio visits revolve around screening, your feedback on how your injury is coping and how you feel, and how we can work on prevention and stability, so that we can minimise the chance of going through all of this again.

Now you have a brief picture of the physio’s perspective, and of the client across the table. Of course, there are a lot of nuances in between, but you can see how a physio shouldn’t just make you lie down on the table for the entire session. It should be interactive, with mutual feedback, and progressive.

If you want to get the best out of your sessions, understand what is going on every step of the way, and be given honest, straightforward feedback and reassurance, then this is the place for you.

References

Himani, Sah, N.K.P., Trivedi, A. and Kanhaiyya (2025) ‘Role of physiotherapy in sports injury prevention and recovery: a comprehensive review’, International Journal of Modern Science and Research Technology, 3(10). Available at: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/396717975_Role_of_Physiotherapy_in_Sports_Injury_Prevention (Accessed: 15 October 2026).

prenatal-training-by-trimester.title: Pre-natal training: what is safe each trimester
prenatal-training-by-trimester.summary: Stay strong and comfortable through pregnancy.
prenatal-training-by-trimester.html:
For most healthy pregnancies, staying active is encouraged. Exercise can support strength, mood, sleep and preparation for birth. Every pregnancy is different though, so always check with your doctor or midwife before you begin or continue a programme.

First trimester

Many women feel tired or nauseous in these early weeks, so energy can vary from day to day. Continue activities you are used to, keep intensity comfortable, and focus on regular walking and moderate strength work.

Second trimester

Energy often returns. This is a good time to build strength in the legs, hips, back and upper body, practise breathing and begin pelvic floor awareness. As your bump grows, exercises are adapted to keep you comfortable and stable.

Third trimester

Training shifts towards maintaining strength, supporting posture and preparing the body for birth. Lower impact, slower tempo and more rest between sets are common. Your trainer will modify any position that feels uncomfortable or makes you dizzy.

Stop and seek medical advice if you notice

  • Vaginal bleeding or leaking fluid
  • Dizziness or feeling faint
  • Chest pain or unusual shortness of breath
  • Calf pain or swelling
  • Regular, painful contractions

After the baby arrives

Returning to exercise after birth should be gradual and guided by your healthcare provider. Post-natal training can rebuild core and pelvic floor function, posture and overall strength at a pace that suits you.
